summary: This unit teaches managers to manage business customers. You will learn how business buyers decide, how to group customers and plan for key accounts, how to measure customer profit, lifetime value and retention, how to use CRM and service agreements, how to communicate, negotiate and handle credit, complaints and feedback, and how to act ethically and protect data.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Business Administration (Management) Level 5 qualification. It is for managers, account managers and supervisors in Jamaican firms and agencies that sell to **business customers**: hotels, schools, hospitals, factories, supermarkets, contractors and public bodies. Business customers buy in larger amounts, over longer periods and with more people involved than members of the public. Managing them means understanding how they buy, deciding which ones matter most, building planned relationships, keeping them satisfied, growing the account and handling problems fairly.

Keeping a business customer is usually cheaper than finding a new one, and a few customers often bring most of the income. This kit follows the order of the work: understand business buyers, group customers and plan for key accounts, measure customer value and profit, use customer records and service agreements, communicate and negotiate, handle complaints and feedback, and act ethically and lawfully.

What this means in your unit
rows: Explain how business-to-business buying differs, and identify who shapes a purchase.
Segment customers and plan key accounts
Group customers by value and need and write an account plan for the most important.
Work out customer profit, lifetime value, retention and churn.
Keep shared records, and agree measurable service levels with customers.
Plan contact, negotiate sensibly and set fair credit terms.
Respond quickly, fix the cause and use surveys and net promoter scores.
Cross-sell and upsell only where there is a real need.
Avoid improper gifts, protect confidential and personal data, and end relationships professionally.

ul: A multiple-choice theory paper with scenarios and sums on retention, profit, lifetime value and net promoter score.
A written paper with short answers (B2B, CRM, SLA, DMU, NPS, churn, gatekeeper) and longer answers where you plan an account, a negotiation or a complaint response.
Group practical tasks: a key account plan, and a role-played quarterly review with a dissatisfied customer.

blocks.note: Work every sum twice. Write the formula first, then the figures, then the unit.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: **B2B** means one business selling to another. An office-supplies distributor that sells to hotels, schools and law firms is trading B2B. Compare it with selling to the public.

head: Feature
Selling to the public
Selling to business customers
rows: Usually one person or a household
Several people, often a group with different roles
Slower, often formal: specifications, quotations, approval
Reliability, quality, service, total cost, risk

blocks.p: The **decision-making unit** is the group of people in a buying firm who together shape a purchase. The roles may be held by one person or by several.

head: Role
What the person does
Example
rows: A plant manager asks for a new supplier of lubricant
The production supervisor who tests a sample and reports on it
Makes or approves the final choice
The finance director who signs for large amounts
Controls access to information and decision-makers
The personal assistant who screens emails and calls

blocks.p: Learn **who is who**, what each cares about, and how to reach them respectfully. The user cares about ease of use, the buyer about price and terms, the decider about cost and risk, and the gatekeeper about not wasting the boss's time.

blocks.h: Know the customer before you meet

ul: The customer's business: what it does, its size, its customers and plans.
What it buys now, from whom and at what price.
Its buying process, approval limits and timing (budget cycles).
Its problems that your product could solve.
Its past dealings with your firm.

blocks.note: Before a first meeting with the purchasing manager of a large hotel, find out the hotel's needs, current suppliers and buying process. Do not arrive with only a price list.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Segmenting customers and managing key accounts

blocks.p: The **Pareto principle**, also called the 80/20 rule, suggests that a small share of customers often brings most of the sales or profit. Check your own records. If 60 of 300 accounts supply most of the gross profit, those 60 deserve closer service and planned contact.

head: Tier
Typical customers
How to serve them
rows: The few that bring a large share of income or profit, or have special strategic value
A named account manager, an account plan, regular reviews, contacts at several levels
A planned visit and call schedule, a named contact
Regular but lighter contact, a sales team or inside sales
Low-cost service: online ordering, phone, standard terms

blocks.p: Review the tiers every year. A customer can move up or down. A small customer that is growing fast may deserve more attention than a larger one that is shrinking.
An **account plan** sets objectives and actions to grow and keep an account. It should contain:

ol: A profile of the customer: business, size, plans, its DMU and contacts.
The history: sales, margins, cost to serve, complaints and satisfaction scores.
The customer's needs and problems, and how you can help.
A relationship map: who in your firm knows whom in theirs.
Objectives (for example, keep on-time delivery above 98%, and grow sales of related products by 10%).
Actions with owners, dates and budget.
Risks (a rival's offer, a change of buyer) and how to manage them.

blocks.h: A relationship map and a team

blocks.p: Do not depend on one contact. Link several of your staff with different staff at the customer: the account manager with the purchasing manager, the operations lead with the user department, the finance officer with accounts payable. When one person leaves, on either side, the relationship survives.

head: Method
Meaning
Example
rows: Selling different products to the same customer
A stationery supplier also offers printer servicing
Persuading the customer to buy a larger or better version
Offering a higher grade of lubricant that lasts longer
The share of the customer's spending in a category that comes to you
The customer spends J$30,000,000 a year on packaging; you supply J$12,000,000: 40%. A target of 55% is J$16,500,000
Moving from yearly to multi-year contracts
A two-year supply contract with agreed prices

blocks.note: Only offer more where the customer has a **real need**. Pushing products the customer does not need damages trust and may lose the account.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Sales are not profit. To judge an account, deduct the cost of the goods **and the cost to serve**: delivery, visits, credit, returns, support, administration.

head: Line
J$
rows: Sales to the customer in a year
Cost to serve (delivery, visits, credit, support)
Profit as a percentage of sales (630,000 ÷ 8,400,000)

blocks.p: Check: 5,880,000 + 1,890,000 = 7,770,000 costs; 8,400,000 − 7,770,000 = 630,000. A large customer can be **unprofitable** if it asks for many small, urgent deliveries. Before dropping such a customer, discuss ordering patterns and terms: minimum order sizes, scheduled deliveries, delivery charges, or price changes. Many unprofitable accounts can be made profitable.
**CLV** is the total profit a firm expects to earn from a customer over the whole relationship. A simple version: orders per year × average order value × gross margin × years of the relationship.

Example: a client places 5 orders a year at an average of J$180,000, the gross margin is 30%, and the client is expected to stay 4 years. 5 × 180,000 = 900,000 sales a year; × 30% = J$270,000 a year; × 4 years = **J$1,080,000**. This tells you how much effort and money it is sensible to spend on keeping the customer.

head: Measure
How to work it out
Worked example
rows: (Customers at start − customers lost) ÷ customers at start × 100. New customers are **not** counted.
A firm begins with 150 accounts, loses 15 and wins 35: (150 − 15) ÷ 150 = 135 ÷ 150 = 90%
Sales from the same customers this year ÷ their sales last year × 100
Retained customers spent J$40,000,000 last year and J$36,000,000 this year: 90%

blocks.p: Retention can look healthy while income falls: the customers who stay may buy less. Track both **customers kept** and **sales per customer**. Winning a new customer usually costs more than keeping one, which is why retention is worth effort.

A **CRM system** is software that records every contact, order, quotation, complaint and note about each customer in one shared place. A shared system matters because, when each salesperson keeps details in a notebook or phone, the firm loses the knowledge when that person leaves.

head: Benefits
Risks and how to manage them
rows: Any authorised staff can see the full history
Contact history stays with the firm when people leave
Managers can spot accounts whose orders have fallen
Follow-ups are less likely to be missed
Cost and training time: train staff and start simply
Poor data if people do not use it: set rules, find out why people avoid it and fix the causes
Data protection: limit access and keep it secure
Too much complexity: record only what is useful

blocks.p: Useful CRM reports include: accounts with orders that have dropped sharply over three months (early warning of loss), sales by customer and product, quotations awaiting reply, overdue invoices, and complaints by cause.
An **SLA** is a written agreement that sets out the standard of service the customer can expect. A good SLA includes:

ul: What is covered: services, hours and sites.
Measurable standards: response time, delivery time, accuracy, uptime.
How performance will be measured and reported, so both sides judge it in the same way.
What happens when standards are missed (credits, corrective action).
Review dates and how to change the agreement.
Responsibilities of the customer (for example, access to the site).

head: Weak service promise
Measurable SLA standard
rows: Phone calls answered within 15 minutes between 7 a.m. and 6 p.m.
98% of orders delivered by the agreed date, measured monthly from signed delivery notes
We will keep the site clean
Daily checks signed by the supervisor; a monthly score above 90% on the agreed checklist

blocks.note: Record each SLA result in the CRM. Customers judge you by what happens, not by what you promised.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Plan how, when and with whom you will keep in touch with each key account. An agreed mix works best: regular **account reviews** (monthly or quarterly), written updates, contact at each level and prompt notice of problems. When a delay will affect a client, **tell the client at once**, explain and give a new date. Never wait for them to find out.

The purpose is to check results against the plan and agree next steps. Prepare the figures (sales, service level results, complaints, open orders), listen first, ask questions and agree actions with owners and dates. If a client says a rival offers the same service for less, **ask questions** to learn what is being compared (scope, quality, terms) before responding with price.

ul: Check the customer's **credit standing** before giving credit: trade references, bank reference, payment history, financial statements.
Set a **credit limit** and terms (for example 30 days) in writing.
Invoice promptly and accurately; send reminders before the due date.
Follow up early and politely when payment is late; agree a payment plan if needed.
Consider a deposit for new or risky customers, and a discount for early payment.
Escalate in line with the firm's procedure.

blocks.p: Credit has a cost. If your firm's money costs 1% a month and a customer who buys J$6,000,000 each month is given 90 days instead of 30 (60 extra days, 2 extra months), the extra cost on each month's order is 6,000,000 × 1% × 2 = J$120,000.

flow: Prepare the facts: sales, margin and cost to serve of the account
Set your aims, your lowest acceptable terms and your best option if there is no deal
Understand the customer's position: why it wants a change, what it values, what rivals offer
Open with the value you bring, not with a price cut
Trade concessions: give a smaller discount only in return for something, such as a longer term or larger volume
Agree and confirm in writing, and record in the CRM

blocks.p: The aim is an agreement that **protects value for both sides**. A big discount that destroys your margin may win the order but lose the profit. Know the point at which you will walk away.

blocks.note: Never give a concession without getting something in return. A discount in exchange for a two-year term or larger volumes is a trade. A discount for nothing is a gift.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.h: Handling a complaint from a business customer

flow: Respond promptly, the same day if possible; acknowledge the problem and apologise for the inconvenience
Listen and find out exactly what happened and what it cost the customer
Offer a clear solution with a date, and a fair remedy
Do it, and check that the customer is satisfied
Find the root cause and change the process

blocks.p: A complaint handled well can **strengthen** the relationship. Do not blame people in front of the customer and do not make promises you cannot keep. Fixing one complaint is not enough: **find the root cause and change the process** so that the same fault does not occur with other accounts. Log complaints by cause (late delivery, wrong item, billing error) and look for the largest causes first.

head: Method
Best for
rows: Short survey after each job or delivery
Annual survey, including the net promoter question
Deep, honest feedback from key accounts

blocks.p: Send surveys to **decision-makers as well as users**: they often see the service differently. If nothing changes after a survey, customers soon stop bothering to reply. Always tell customers what you did with their answers.

Ask: "How likely are you to recommend us to a colleague?" on a scale of 0 to 10. Scores of 9 and 10 are **promoters**, 7 and 8 are **passives** and 0 to 6 are **detractors**. **NPS = % promoters − % detractors** (passives are ignored). Example: 55% promoters, 25% passives, 20% detractors: NPS = 55 − 20 = **35**. NPS can range from −100 to +100.
A rise in satisfaction scores while large accounts still leave may mean that the survey is not reaching the people who decide.

blocks.h: Measures of how well you manage customers

ul: Customer retention rate and churn, and revenue per key account.
Sales growth per key account and share of wallet.
Customer profit and the cost to serve.
Service level results and on-time delivery.
Complaints (number, cause, time to resolve) and NPS.
Overdue payments (days sales outstanding).

sections.title: Ethics, confidentiality, data protection and ending relationships

ul: **Gifts and hospitality:** a buyer who hints that a personal gift would help win a contract is asking for a bribe. Decline, record it and report it under company policy. Small, open, policy-approved courtesies, such as a diary or a modest lunch, are different from private gifts meant to influence a decision.

**Confidentiality:** information a client shares (plans, prices, volumes) must not be passed to its competitors, even if they are your customers too. Do not discuss one customer's prices with another.
**Honesty:** do not promise dates or results the firm cannot deliver, and do not hide a problem to protect a sale.
**Conflicts of interest:** declare any personal tie to a client or its rivals.
**Fair dealing:** treat all customers by the same rules; do not pressure buyers.

blocks.p: Names, phone numbers, emails and other details of contacts at your business customers are **personal data**. Keep them secure, use them only for the purposes for which they were given and share them only with those who need them. In line with the data protection law, do not hand client contact lists to marketing partners without agreement, and do not store client records on personal phones or unprotected devices. If records are lost or stolen, **report it at once** under the firm's data breach procedure.

When an account manager leaves, plan a **handover**: joint visits to introduce the new manager, full CRM notes, the account plan, open issues and a message to the client. Do not let the account depend on one person's memory.

Sometimes a customer remains unprofitable, refuses to change terms or behaves unreasonably. Ending the relationship is a last resort, after discussing the problems and offering options. Do it professionally: **give notice under the contract**, explain your reasons, honour existing orders and help with a handover to another supplier. Avoid damaging your reputation.

blocks.note: Do not carry on with an account at a loss without a plan to fix it, and do not drop it without studying the numbers and talking to the customer first.
blocks.label: Tip

terms: B2B
Business-to-business: trade between one business and another.
Decision-making unit (DMU)
The group of people in a buying firm who shape a purchase.
Gatekeeper
The person who controls access to information and decision-makers.
Influencer
A person whose advice shapes the decision.
Pareto principle
The 80/20 rule: a small share of customers often brings most of the sales.
Key account
A customer so important that it has its own plan and manager.
Account plan
A plan of objectives and actions to keep and grow an account.
Cross-selling
Selling different products to the same customer.
Upselling
Persuading a customer to buy a bigger or better version.
Share of wallet
The share of a customer's spending in a category that comes to you.
Cost to serve
The cost of delivery, visits, credit and support for an account.
Customer lifetime value (CLV)
The total profit expected from a customer over the relationship.
Retention rate
The percentage of customers kept over a period.
Churn
The rate at which customers stop buying.
CRM
Customer relationship management: a system for recording all contact with customers.
SLA
Service level agreement: a written, measurable standard of service.
Net promoter score (NPS)
Percentage of promoters minus percentage of detractors.
Root cause
The basic reason a problem happened.
Data breach
Loss or unauthorised access to personal data.

c1.title: A packaging supplier in Mandeville
c1.text: A Mandeville packaging firm supplies a bottling plant. Last year sales to the plant were J$8,400,000, the cost of the goods was J$5,880,000 and the cost to serve the account (many small urgent deliveries, extra visits and support) was J$1,890,000. The firm has 100 business accounts, and its records show that the top 20 supply 75% of gross profit. The account manager is Mr Clive Bennett.

c2.title: An IT support firm in Kingston
c2.text: A Kingston IT support firm began the year with 250 business clients, lost 25 and won 40. Its annual survey of IT officers at the clients gave 45% promoters, 35% passives and 20% detractors. The managing director, Ms Andrea Wright, notes that retention is up on last year but that revenue is flat, and that several clients who left had given high scores in the survey.

c3.title: An industrial supplier in Portmore
c3.text: An industrial supplier in Portmore sells packaging materials to a large garment factory. The factory spends J$30,000,000 a year on packaging, of which the supplier provides J$12,000,000. The plant manager proposed changing suppliers, the production supervisor tests samples and gives advice, the purchasing officer places orders and the finance director approves large contracts. The supplier's account manager, Mr Ian Gordon, wants to raise its share of the factory's packaging spending to 55%.

c4.title: A food distributor in St Catherine
c4.text: A St Catherine food distributor sells J$6,000,000 of goods each month to a supermarket group on 30-day terms. The group now asks for 90 days. The distributor's cost of money is 1% a month. Last week a delivery was short by 40 cartons, and the supermarket missed a weekend promotion. The account manager, Ms Sherene Francis, has to reply.

c5.title: A corporate caterer in Kingston
c5.text: A Kingston corporate catering firm serves several companies. A client's buyer asks the account manager, Mr Garth Powell, for the prices the firm charges another client "for comparison". Before Christmas a staff member wants to send a large personal gift to a buyer. Sales staff keep client contacts in their own phones and personal messaging groups, and a marketing partner has asked for the full contact list to promote its own services.

questions.q: What was the profit on the bottling plant account after the cost to serve?
questions.why: Sales J$8,400,000 − goods J$5,880,000 = gross profit J$2,520,000. Less cost to serve J$1,890,000 = J$630,000. Gross profit alone overstates what the account earns.

questions.q: What is the account's profit as a percentage of sales?
questions.why: 630,000 ÷ 8,400,000 = 0.075, so 7.5%. Gross margin is 30%, but after cost to serve only 7.5% remains.

questions.q: Mr Bennett finds that many small urgent deliveries raise the cost to serve. What is the best first step?
o: Drop the plant at once to stop the loss of margin
Add a hidden charge to each delivery without telling the plant
Ask the delivery team to work longer hours at no extra cost
Discuss ordering patterns and offer scheduled deliveries
questions.why: The cost drivers can often be changed by agreement: minimum orders, scheduled deliveries, delivery charges. Talk first, then decide. Hidden charges damage trust and may breach the contract.

questions.q: The firm's top 20 accounts supply 75% of gross profit. How should it use this fact?
o: Give all 100 accounts the same number of visits each year
Give the top 20 key account plans and light service to the rest
Stop serving the 80 smaller accounts to save time and money
Allocate visits to accounts by the date each account opened
questions.why: The Pareto pattern means attention should follow value. The top accounts deserve plans, named managers and reviews. Small accounts need efficient low-cost service, not neglect.

questions.q: What was the firm's churn rate for the year, and how many clients did it have at the end?
o: 10%, and 225 clients
10%, and 265 clients
16%, and 265 clients
90%, and 290 clients
questions.why: Churn = clients lost ÷ clients at the start = 25 ÷ 250 = 10% (retention is the other 90%). Clients at the end = 250 − 25 + 40 = 265.

questions.q: One client answers the net promoter question with a score of 8 out of 10. How is this answer counted?
o: As a promoter, because 8 is a high score
As a detractor, because it is not a 9 or 10
As half a promoter and half a detractor
As a passive, neither a promoter nor a detractor
questions.why: Scores of 9 and 10 are promoters, 7 and 8 are passives and 0 to 6 are detractors. Passives are counted in the total of replies but do not enter the promoter-minus-detractor calculation.

questions.q: Several clients who left had given high scores. What is the most likely reason?
o: The survey reached IT officers, not those who decide
The scores were too high to be accurate or useful
The clients who left had never actually used the service
High scores always mean that a client will stay
questions.why: Users and decision-makers often see service differently. A survey reaching only IT officers may miss the managers who decide whether to renew. Survey both groups.

questions.q: Retention is up but revenue is flat. Which explanation is most likely?
o: The firm has taken on too many new clients this year
The survey scores of the clients are too low
Kept clients may be buying less, so sales per client fell
Retention and revenue are always measured in the same way
questions.why: Retention counts customers, not spending. Clients can stay but reduce what they buy. Track revenue retention and sales per client as well.

questions.q: The plant manager proposed changing suppliers. Which role in the decision-making unit is this?
o: Gatekeeper
Decider
User
Initiator
questions.why: The initiator starts the idea of buying or changing. The decider makes or approves the final choice, and the gatekeeper controls access.

questions.q: The finance director approves large contracts. Which role is this?
o: Influencer
Decider
Initiator
Gatekeeper
questions.why: The person who makes or approves the final decision is the decider. The purchasing officer is the buyer, and the production supervisor who advises is an influencer.

questions.q: What is the supplier's current share of the factory's packaging spending, and what sales does 55% mean?
questions.why: 12,000,000 ÷ 30,000,000 = 40%. 55% of J$30,000,000 = 0.55 × 30,000,000 = J$16,500,000. Share of wallet is the supplier's sales divided by the customer's total spend in the category.

questions.q: Mr Gordon offers a longer-lasting, higher-grade carton to the factory. What is this called, and when is it sound?
o: Upselling, if it meets a need the factory has shown
Cross-selling, if the factory dislikes its present cartons
Upselling, if it makes the supplier's own margin larger
Cross-selling, if the new cartons cost the factory less
questions.why: Selling a better or larger version of what the customer already buys is upselling. It is sound when it meets a real need shown by the customer, not simply to raise the supplier's margin.

questions.q: What is the extra cost of financing the longer credit period on each month's sales?
questions.why: The extra time is 60 days, or 2 months. 1% a month × 2 = 2%. 2% of J$6,000,000 = J$120,000.

questions.q: What should Ms Francis do before agreeing to 90 days?
o: Agree at once, because the group is a large customer
Agree, but leave the terms without a written change
Check credit standing, set a limit and written terms
Refuse to discuss credit terms with a customer of any size
questions.why: Credit is a risk and a cost. A check of credit standing, a limit and written terms protect the firm. A concession should be traded for something, such as volume or a longer contract.

questions.q: The delivery was short by 40 cartons and the supermarket missed a promotion. What is the best first response?
o: Wait for the supermarket's accounts department to chase her
Reply at once, apologise, learn the impact, offer a dated fix
Blame the driver and give his name to the supermarket
Say the shortage is a count error made by the supermarket
questions.why: A quick, honest reply shows respect and limits damage. Establish the facts and impact, and give a clear, dated solution. Blaming people or denying without checking worsens the problem.

questions.q: After the complaint is solved, what will best stop it happening with other accounts?
o: Give a larger discount to every supermarket customer
Stop recording complaints to avoid extra paperwork
Tell the driver to be more careful in future deliveries
Find the root cause and change the checking process
questions.why: A root cause fix changes the process, so the fault does not recur for any account. Logging and analysing complaints shows the largest causes.

questions.q: A client's buyer asks for another client's prices. What should Mr Powell do?
o: Give them, because the buyer asked politely and openly
Refuse politely, because prices are confidential
Give approximate figures only, to be helpful
Give them only if the other client is a competitor
questions.why: Confidential information about one customer must not be passed to another. Doing so breaks trust and may breach agreements. Offer to prepare a fair quotation for this client instead.

questions.q: A staff member wants to send a large personal gift to a buyer before Christmas. What is the correct approach?
o: Follow the gifts policy: modest, open and approved only
Send it from his own pocket so that it stays private
Send it after the contract has been renewed
Send it, and record the gift as a business cost
questions.why: A large private gift to a buyer may be seen as an attempt to influence a decision, and may be a bribe. A gifts policy sets limits and requires openness and approval.

questions.q: Sales staff keep client contacts in personal phones and messaging groups. What should the firm do?
o: Leave it as it is, because the staff are trustworthy
Move all the contacts to one staff member's own phone
Print the contacts and keep the sheets in the office
Move it to a secure shared system with access controls
questions.why: Client contact details are personal data and must be kept secure. A shared system with access controls and a proper record also keeps the knowledge in the firm when staff leave.

questions.q: The marketing partner asks for the full contact list. What is the correct response?
o: Send the list, because the partner is also a business
Send only the phone numbers, not the email addresses
Refuse unless the contacts have agreed to the use
Offer the list for sale to other interested firms
questions.why: Personal data may be used only for the purposes for which it was given. Sharing with a partner needs agreement and a lawful reason, in line with the data protection law.
